title: Drift Velocity and Resistivity Relations

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Current Electricity

expression: I = nAqvd  ;  R = ρL/A  ;  ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T−T₀)]
explanation: Current in terms of microscopic quantities: I = nAqvd (n = free charge carrier density, A = cross-sectional area, q = charge per carrier, vd = drift velocity). Resistance R = ρL/A shows resistance depends on BOTH the intrinsic material property resistivity ρ AND the conductor's geometry (length, area), while ρ itself depends only on the material and temperature. For most metals, resistivity increases nearly linearly with temperature via the temperature coefficient α.

workedExample.scenario: A copper wire of resistivity 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, length 2 m, area 1×10⁻⁶ m².

commonMistakes: Confusing resistivity (material property, Ω·m) with resistance (depends on geometry too, Ω) — a very common source of error when a wire is reshaped/stretched.
Assuming resistivity always increases with temperature — this holds for metals, but semiconductors show the OPPOSITE trend (resistivity decreases with rising temperature).
genZNote: Resistivity is the material's personality trait; resistance also cares about its shape.
